content: Each gram of human feces contains approximately 10 billion bacteria. Among these, there may be pathogenic bacteria, such as Salmonella, which is associated with gastroenteritis. In addition to bacteria, feces may also harbor pathogenic viruses, protozoa, and parasites. If these organisms are ingested, they have the potential to cause disease. When testing drinking water for contamination, the wide variety and often low concentrations of pathogens make it challenging to test for each pathogen individually. As a result, health authorities rely on the presence of other, more abundant and more easily detectable fecal bacteria as indicators of fecal contamination. These indicator bacteria are not inherently harmful to human health but serve as markers for the potential presence of health risks. The most commonly recognized indicator bacteria are fecal coliforms, which are found in the intestinal tracts of warm-blooded animals. Another, less frequently used group of indicator organisms includes hydrogen sulfide-producing bacteria. These bacteria are also present in humans, as well as in the intestinal tracts of birds and reptiles, which are known carriers of Salmonella. The World Health Organization (WHO) Guidelines for Drinking Water Quality state that the presence of Escherichia coli (E. coli) as an indicator organism provides definitive evidence of recent fecal contamination. E. coli should not be present in water intended for human consumption. It is generally accepted that the higher the number of coliform organisms detected in a 100 mL water sample, the greater the risk of waterborne disease.
